claims.text: The target HfNbTaTiZr sample is a single-phase alloy.
The target sample can be treated as defect-free and have oxygen content below 0.15 wt.%.
The new approach uses machine-learned force fields trained on DFT and molecular-dynamics simulations.
The proposed force-field approach can independently quantify phonon disorder and electronic transport mechanisms.
Chemical disorder causes lattice distortions in HfNbTaTiZr.
Force-constant fluctuations are a dominant source of phonon scattering in the relevant high-entropy alloy.
The phonon-scattering effects of disorder are distinct from electronic scattering mechanisms.
Separately modeling force-constant fluctuations and electronic conduction avoids the oversimplification of a single Debye-temperature treatment.
Separating lattice and electronic transport produces a more physically accurate estimate of lattice thermal conductivity.
A cocktail effect influences electron mobility in HfNbTaTiZr.
The predicted lattice thermal conductivity will be 30–50% lower than estimates from conventional unified Debye-based models.
The 30–50% reduction is expected particularly between 300 and 600 K.
The lattice thermal conductivity will have weak temperature dependence below 200 K.
The lattice thermal conductivity will increase nonlinearly above 300 K.
Prior approaches use a Debye temperature together with linear combinations of elemental properties.
Prior approaches typically overestimate lattice thermal conductivity because they conflate lattice and electronic contributions.
Substantial oxygen contamination can prevent formation of a single-phase random solid solution in HfNbTaTiZr.
Oxygen contamination and other defects alter the thermal-scattering mechanisms relevant to the model.
A phonon-electron transport crossover occurs near 200 K.
Failure to observe a 30–50% lattice-conductivity reduction relative to a conventional Debye-based prediction would falsify the hypothesis.
